title: Better and Saner Grading Tip: Get Out the Stopwatch
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart offers a concrete method for taming the workload of grading student writing: time each paper with a stopwatch. He walks through seven steps, from sitting down with only the stack and rubrics, to grading five papers with lap timing, taking a break, and then analyzing which activities fail to help students become better writers. The benefits he lists are sustained focus, faster decisions, less urge to copyedit, and the ability to predict how long a whole stack will take. That predictability lets him schedule one-hour grading blocks and return work promptly without the guilt of the stack. The piece is about teacher workload and sustainable professional habits rather than assessment theory, which is why it sits with the craft of the job.
points: Timing each paper with a lap-capable stopwatch turns grading from a vague dread into a measurable task.
Reviewing the lap times shows which grading habits do not help students and can be satisficed or skipped.
The time limit forces decisions and curbs over-commenting and copyediting.
Knowing the average minutes per paper allows scheduling grading in one-hour blocks and returning work on time.
quotes: I don't have all the answers when it comes to taming the beast that is grading student writing, but here's something that I have found to help this year: using a stopwatch.
Step Three: Start the stopwatch and grade an essay. Do whatever it is that you do when you grade this kind of essay. Make comments, mark things, write on the rubric, assign a percentage, etc.

Are any of the things you do during a grading lap unlikely to help your students become better writers? Might you experiment with satisficing those things (or skipping them altogether) in the next round of five papers so as to improve your pace?

Timing forces quicker decision-making. I can't dither about what to write or not write; I just have to move forward with the task of helping this writer (my Want to Do) and assigning a score (my Have to Do).
Timing pushes back the urge to cover a paper with comments and markings. Me acting as a professional copyeditor is, at the risk of overgeneralizing, a pointless waste of my time.
No more wondering, no more dreading — I just know that this will take three more hours because I have 45 more papers and each paper takes me an average of four minutes to grade.
